The '''Pratt & Whitney PW1000G''' family, also marketed as the '''Pratt & Whitney GTF''' (geared turbofan), is a family of high-bypass [[geared turbofan]] engines produced by [[Pratt & Whitney]]. The various models can generate 15,000 to 33,000 [[Pound (force)|pounds-force]] (67 to 147 [[Newton (unit)|kilonewtons]]) of thrust. As of 2025, they are used on the [[Airbus A220]], [[Airbus A320neo family]], and [[Embraer E-Jet E2]]. They were also used on new [[Yakovlev MC-21|Yakovlev MC-21s]] until exports to Russia were stopped as part of the [[International sanctions during the Russian invasion of Ukraine|international sanctions during the invasion of Ukraine]].

Following years of development and testing on various demonstrators, the program officially launched in 2008 with the PW1200G destined for the later-canceled [[Mitsubishi SpaceJet]]. The first successful flight test occurred later that year. The PW1500G variant, designed for the A220, became the first certified engine in 2013. P&W is estimated to have spent $10 billion to develop the engine family. The type certificate for the PW1100G is held by [[International Aero Engines]] while the other versions are held by Pratt & Whitney.

Unlike traditional turbofan engines whose single shaft forces all components to turn at the same speed, the PW1000G has a [[gearbox]] between the fan and the low-pressure core. This allows each section to operate at its optimal speed. Pratt & Whitney says this enables the PW1000G to use 16% less fuel and produce 75% less noise than previous generation engines.

The engine family initially garnered interest from airlines due to its fuel efficiency, but technical problems have hurt its standing in the market. For example, early problems with the PW1100G variant, which powers the A320neo family, grounded aircraft and caused in-flight failures. Some engines were built with contaminated [[Powder metallurgy|powdered metal]], requiring repairs of 250 to 300 days. Some airlines chose the [[CFM LEAP]] engine instead.

==Development==

===Precursors===
Wind tunnel tests were conducted at the [[NASA Glenn]] Research Center in the late 1980s using Pratt & Whitney’s 17-inch diameter ducted fan model. In summer 1993, Pratt & Whitney started to test its {{cvt|53,000|lbf|kN}} Advanced Ducted Propulsor (ADP) demonstrator at the [[NASA Ames]] {{cvt|40|-|80|ft}} Wind Tunnel, using a 4:1, {{cvt|40,000|hp|MW}} gearbox.<!--<ref name=AvWeek26jul1993>-->
Its {{cvt|118.2|in|cm}} fan with 18 [[Variable-pitch propeller (aeronautics)|reversing pitch]] composite blades had a 15:1 bypass ratio.<!--<ref name=AvWeek26jul1993>-->
It aimed to cut fuel consumption by 6–7%, emissions by 15%, and generate less noise due to lower fan tip speed of {{cvt|950|ft/s}}, down from {{cvt|1,400|ft/s}} in conventional 5:1 bypass turbofans.<!--<ref name=AvWeek26jul1993>-->
While the gearbox and larger fan weighed more, this was mitigated by using 40% composites by weight, up from 15%.<!--<ref name=AvWeek26jul1993>-->
In 1994 P&W was planning to run a {{cvt|60,000|hp|MW}} gearbox for {{cvt|75,000|lbf|kN}} of thrust.<ref name=AvWeek26jul1993>{{cite magazine |url= http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19930726/#!&pid=40 |title= Pratt & Whitney starts new ADP test phase |magazine= Aviation Week |page= 40 |date= July 26, 1993 |url-access= subscription |access-date= March 20, 2018 |archive-date= March 20, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180320230809/http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19930726/#!&pid=40 |url-status= live }}</ref> Additional model scale tests of the ADP were conducted in the NASA Glenn {{cvt|9|-|15|ft}} Low-Speed Wind Tunnel from 1995 through 1997 to investigate lower fan tip speeds and lower fan pressure ratios.<ref name=NASAtests> {{cite journal |last1=Huff |first1=Dennis|date=April 2013 |title=NASA Glenn's Contributions to Aircraft Engine Noise Research |url=https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000283 |journal=Journal of Aerospace Engineering |volume=26 |issue=2 |publisher=American Society of Civil Engineers |pages=237–238 |doi=10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000283 |access-date=August 29, 2025 |url-access= subscription|hdl=2060/20150000139 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

P&W first attempted to build a production geared turbofan starting around 1998, with the PW8000,<ref name=Interavia199806>{{cite magazine |issn=1423-3215 |id={{ProQuest|195925457}} |url= http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-20944971.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20121019125946/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-20944971.html |archive-date= October 19, 2012 |title= Pratt & Whitney's surprise leap |magazine= [[Interavia (magazine)|Interavia Business & Technology]] |publisher= [[Highbeam Research]] |first1= Bill |last1= Sweetman |first2= Oliver |last2= Sutton |volume=53 |number=621 |pages=25–26 |publication-date= June 1998}}</ref> targeted for the {{cvt|25,000–35,000|lbf|kN}} range. This was an upgrade of the existing [[Pratt & Whitney PW6000|PW6000]] that replaced the fan section with a gear box and a new single-stage fan, which would provide about 90% of the propulsive power of the engine. The PW8000 engine aimed for 10% lower operating costs, or $600,000 per aircraft annually.<ref name="SAEI1998">{{cite magazine |issn=0736-2536 |url= http://www.sae.org/aeromag/techinnovations/1298t10.htm |publisher= SAE International |title= Pratt & Whitney's next leap in engine technology |magazine= Aerospace Engineering Magazine Online |at= Top 15 Technology Innovations |date= 1998 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20000420023434/http://www.sae.org/aeromag/techinnovations/1298t10.htm |archive-date= 20 April 2000 }}</ref>

The PW8000 had an 11:1 [[bypass ratio]] (twice that of the [[V2500]]), a 40:1 [[overall pressure ratio]], and 13 rotor stages instead of the 17 <ref>{{cite web |url= http://i-a-e.com/products.html |publisher= International Aero Engines |title= Products}}</ref> in the V2500 for similar thrusts.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998>-->
Preliminary development was to end by June 1, the first test for 10 months later, and certification 20 months after, for $400 million.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998>-->
Pratt had tested gearboxes for 950 hours for $350 million in the previous decade and aimed for 99.5% efficiency.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998>-->
The ADP gearbox was 30% more powerful and the reversing pitch fan was not retained for the PW8000.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998>-->
P&W was to control 60% of the program, shared with IAE partners MTU and FiatAvio but not Rolls-Royce, and possibly with Volvo and MHI.<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998>{{cite magazine |url= http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19980223/#!&pid=32 |title= Pratt & Whitney Launches Geared Turbofan Engine |magazine= Aviation Week |page= 32 |date= Feb 23, 1998 |url-access= subscription |access-date= March 20, 2018 |archive-date= March 21, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180321063041/http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19980223/#!&pid=32 |url-status= live }}</ref>

Its {{abbr|LP|low pressure}} turbine ran at 9,160 rpm, reduced by 3:1 for a 3,250 rpm fan having a {{cvt|1,050|ft/s}} blade tip speed down from {{cvt|1,400|ft/s}}, dropping noise to 30 EPNdB cumulated below Stage 3 requirements.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34>-->
The {{cvt|76–79|in|cm}} fan had 20 [[titanium]] blades, and moved {{cvt|1,369|lb}} of air per second in climb.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34>-->
The conventional 3-stage {{abbr|LP|low pressure}} compressor was followed by a 5-stage, 12:1 {{abbr|HP|high pressure}} compressor fitted with 700 blades inspired by the military {{abbr|ATEGG|advanced turbine engine gas generator}} program's low aspect-ratio airfoils.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34>-->
A floatwall/TALON combustor was followed by a single stage HP turbine and a counter rotating 3-stage LP turbine with 400 blades, both [[computational fluid dynamics]] (CFD) optimized.<!--<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34>-->
The gearbox could handle {{cvt|50|hp/lb}}.<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34/> The physical size of the gearbox was {{convert|17|in}} in diameter,<ref name=Interavia199806/> or no more than half the gearbox size of the [[PW-Allison 578-DX]] propfan demonstrator engine that Pratt & Whitney worked jointly on with [[Allison Engine Company|Allison]] in the 1980s. The gearbox consisted of 40 components, weighed {{cvt|500|lb}}, and shared a {{convert|3|usgal|l|adj=mid|sp=us}} oil tank with the rest of the engine. The efficiency of the gearbox was 99.7%.<ref name="ATW199808">{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Air Transport World]] |issn=0002-2543 |title=Inside the (gear) box thinking |id={{ProQuest|224262414}} |volume=35 |number=8 |publication-date=August 1998 |page=51}}</ref> Eight engines would have been used for certification.<ref name=AvWeek23feb1998p34>{{cite magazine |url= http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19980223/#!&pid=34 |title= Geared-turbofan engine design targets cost, complexity |magazine= Aviation Week |page= 34 |date= Feb 23, 1998 |url-access= subscription |access-date= March 20, 2018 |archive-date= March 21, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180321063041/http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/19980223/#!&pid=34 |url-status= live }}</ref>
After several years, the PW8000 project was abandoned.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://cornponepapers.blogspot.com/2006/04/short-life-and-untimely-demise-of.html |date= April 17, 2006 |title= The Short Life and Untimely Demise of the PW8000 |work= The Dougloid Papers |author= Robert Luedeman |access-date= April 11, 2008 |archive-date= July 8, 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110708031910/http://cornponepapers.blogspot.com/2006/04/short-life-and-untimely-demise-of.html |url-status= live }}{{self-published inline|date=November 2016}}</ref>

Soon afterwards the ATFI project appeared, using a [[PW308]] core but with a new gearbox and a single-stage fan.{{citation needed|date=December 2021}} It had its first run on March 16, 2001.{{citation needed|date=December 2021}} This led to the Geared Turbofan (GTF) program, which was based around a newly designed core jointly developed with German [[MTU Aero Engines]].{{citation needed|date=December 2021}}

===Geared turbofan (GTF)===
[[File:ILA Berlin 2012 PD 142.JPG|thumb|Mockup with compressor and turbine cutaway]]
By 2006, Pratt & Whitney was spending $100 million per year on geared turbofan development for the next generation of [[single-aisle]] airliners, and focusing on the {{cvt|25,000-35,000|lbf|kN}} thrust range.<ref name=Flight7Mar2006/> At the time, P&W was supporting 36% of the engines in the Western-operated commercial fleet, compared to [[CFM International|CFM]]'s 33% (growing), [[GE Aviation|GE]]'s 13%, [[Rolls-Royce plc|Rolls-Royce]]'s 11%, and [[International Aero Engines|IAE]]'s 6% (growing); but it was decreasing as it was mostly based on the older [[JT8D]].<ref name=Flight7Mar2006/>
The company was hoping the GTF could cut [[Thrust-specific fuel consumption|fuel burn]] by up to 12% and noise by 31 dB compared with then-current engines.<ref name=Flight7Mar2006/>
P&W was planning a ground engine demonstration in late 2007, aimed at {{cvt|30,000|lbf|kN}} thrust with a 2 m (80 in)-diameter fan.<ref name=Flight7Mar2006>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/gearing-up-again-pratt-and-whitneys-obsession-with-the-geared-turbofan/66110.article |title= Gearing up again: Pratt & Whitney's obsession with the geared turbofan |date= 7 March 2006 |author= Guy Norris |work= Flight International |archive-date= 13 September 2024 |access-date= 3 December 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20240913085128/https://www.flightglobal.com/gearing-up-again-pratt-and-whitneys-obsession-with-the-geared-turbofan/66110.article |url-status= live }}</ref>
The first ground test of the demonstrator was performed in November 2007 at [[West Palm Beach, Florida]].<ref name="FirstGroundTest">{{cite news |work=Green Car Congress |title=Pratt & Whitney Begins Ground Testing on Geared Turbofan Demonstrator Engine Ahead of Schedule; Targeting 12%+ Improvements in Fuel Burn |url=https://www.greencarcongress.com/2007/11/pratt-whitney-b.html |date=November 15, 2007 |archive-date=November 15, 2020 |access-date=August 22, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201115120508/https://www.greencarcongress.com/2007/11/pratt-whitney-b.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In October 2007, the GTF was selected to power the 70- to 90-seat [[Mitsubishi Regional Jet]] (MRJ).<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/pictures-pratt-and-whitney-geared-turbofan-engine-selected-to-power-mitsubishi-regional-jet/76631.article |title= Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan engine selected to power Mitsubishi Regional Jet |author= Stephen Trimble |date= 9 October 2007 |work= FlightGlobal |archive-date= 8 August 2024 |access-date= 3 December 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20240808140813/https://www.flightglobal.com/pictures-pratt-and-whitney-geared-turbofan-engine-selected-to-power-mitsubishi-regional-jet/76631.article |url-status= live }}</ref>
In March 2008, [[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries]] launched the MRJ with an order for 25 aircraft from [[All Nippon Airways]], then targeting a 2013 entry into service.<ref>{{cite press release |url= https://www.mhi.com/news/200803281230.html |title= MHI Officially Launches Mitsubishi Regional Jet Program |date= March 28, 2008 }}</ref>
In July 2008, the GTF was renamed ''PW1000G'', the first in a new line of "PurePower" engines.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.aero-news.net/index.cfm?do=main.textpost&id=45f9dc70-2d55-450a-9a91-1ed8167f6198 |title= Farnborough '08: Pratt & Whitney Launches PurePower Engine Family |date= Jul 14, 2008 |work= Aero-News Network |archive-date= December 31, 2018 |access-date= November 29, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181231135049/http://www.aero-news.net/index.cfm?do=main.textpost&id=45f9dc70-2d55-450a-9a91-1ed8167f6198 |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Flight testing===
[[File:Boeing 747SP-J6 Pratt & Whitney AN2732961.jpg|thumb|Flight testing on a 747SP, in #2 position]]

The engine was first tested on the Pratt & Whitney [[Boeing 747SP]] on July 11, 2008 through mid-August 2008, totaling 12 flights and 43.5 flight hours.<ref name="Flight20080819">{{cite magazine |magazine=Flight International |given=Jon |surname=Ostrower |date=August 19, 2008 |title=P&W completes GTF tests on 747SP, readies for A340 trial |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-completes-gtf-tests-on-747sp-readies-for-a340-t-314810/ |access-date=July 27, 2019 |archive-date=July 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190727070853/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-completes-gtf-tests-on-747sp-readies-for-a340-t-314810/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It then flew starting October 14, 2008 on an [[Airbus A340]]-600 in Toulouse on the number two pylon.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-owned-a340-flies-pw-geared-turbofan-engine-317447/ |title= Airbus-owned A340 flies P&W geared turbofan engine |date= October 14, 2008 |work= Flight Global |archive-date= January 12, 2019 |access-date= November 29, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190112001910/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-owned-a340-flies-pw-geared-turbofan-engine-317447/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

<!--PW1500G-->
Testing of the CSeries bound PW1524G model began in October 2010.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pratt-whitney-geared-pw1524g-testing-underway-349133/ |date= October 30, 2010 |title= Pratt & Whitney geared PW1524G testing underway |work= Flight Global |archive-date= December 13, 2014 |access-date= November 29, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141213063907/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pratt-whitney-geared-pw1524g-testing-underway-349133/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
In addition to the geared turbofan, the initial designs included a variable-area fan nozzle (VAFN), which allows improvements in propulsive efficiency across a range of the flight envelope.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pampw-readies-for-cseries-third-knob-engine-testing-353585/ |title=P&W readies for CSeries "third knob" engine testing |date= 23 February 2011 |work= Flight Global}}</ref> However, the VAFN has since been dropped from production designs due to high system weight. The PW1500G engine achieved Transport Canada type certification on February 20, 2013.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.41744-transport-canada-certifies-pratt-whitney-purepower-r-pw1500g-engine-for-bombardier-cseries-aircraft.bombardiercom.html |publisher= Bombardier |date= February 13, 2013 |title= Transport Canada Certifies Pratt & Whitney PurePower® PW1500G Engine for Bombardier CSeries Aircraft |access-date= November 29, 2016 |archive-date= January 27, 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210127073018/https://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.41744-transport-canada-certifies-pratt-whitney-purepower-r-pw1500g-engine-for-bombardier-cseries-aircraft.bombardiercom.html |url-status= live }}</ref>
The first flight test on one of its intended production airframes, the [[Bombardier CSeries]] (Airbus A220), was on September 16, 2013.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.bombardier-aerospace20130916cseriesfirstflight.bombardiercom.html |title=Bombardier's CSeries Aircraft Completes Historic First Flight |date= September 16, 2013 |publisher= Bombardier}}</ref>

<!--PW1100G-->
The A320 engine, the PW1100G, had made its first static engine test run on November 1, 2012,<ref>{{cite press release |url= https://www.pw.utc.com/static/files/PW1100G-JM.pdf |publisher= Pratt and Whitney |date= May 15, 2017 |title= PurePower® PW1100G-JM Engine |access-date= May 14, 2019 |archive-date= May 14, 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190514071939/https://www.pw.utc.com/static/files/PW1100G-JM.pdf |url-status= dead }}</ref> and was first tested on the 747SP on May 15, 2013.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/in-focus-pratt-completes-first-flight-of-pw1100g-engine-386605/ |title= IN FOCUS: Pratt completes first flight of PW1100G engine |date= 3 June 2013 |work= Flight Global |archive-date= 10 June 2019 |access-date= 4 June 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190610211940/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/in-focus-pratt-completes-first-flight-of-pw1100g-engine-386605/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
The first flight of the [[Airbus A320neo]] followed on September 25, 2014.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/a320neo-completes-first-flight |title= A320neo Completes First Flight |date= Sep 25, 2014 |work= Aviation Week |access-date= May 20, 2015 |archive-date= September 19, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180919065642/http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/a320neo-completes-first-flight |url-status= dead }}</ref> The PW1100G engine achieved FAA type certification on December 19, 2014.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.purepowerengines.com/press/14121900.htm |title= FAA Certifies PurePower® Engine for A320neo Aircraft |date= December 19, 2014 |publisher= Pratt & Whitney |access-date= January 10, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150110082317/http://www.purepowerengines.com/press/14121900.htm |archive-date= January 10, 2015 }}</ref>
<!--PW1900G-->
The fourth variant of the engine, the PW1900G for the [[Embraer E2]], first flew on November 3, 2015 from [[Montréal–Mirabel International Airport|Mirabel]] in Canada fitted to the Boeing 747SP test aircraft.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-launches-engine-flight-test-campaign-for-new-emb-418560/ |journal= [[Flight International]] |date= 3 November 2015 |page= 12 |title= P&W launches engine flight test campaign for new Embraer jets |archive-date= 11 January 2019 |access-date= 29 November 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190111215908/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-launches-engine-flight-test-campaign-for-new-emb-418560/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Production ===
[[File:Bombardier CS100 (26889780191).jpg|thumb|Underneath the wing of an [[Airbus A220|A220]]  with cowlings open]]

The program cost is estimated at $10 billion.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/technology/boeing-s-nma-poses-propulsion-puzzle-engine-makers |title= Boeing's NMA Poses Propulsion Puzzle For Engine Makers |date= Jun 2, 2017 |author= Guy Norris |work= Aviation Week & Space Technology |archive-date= October 18, 2018 |access-date= June 7, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181018074435/http://aviationweek.com/technology/boeing-s-nma-poses-propulsion-puzzle-engine-makers |url-status= live }}</ref>
The list price was ${{#expr:1030/86round1}} million in 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2011-12-14/jetblue-to-buy-pratt-whitney-engines |title= JetBlue Picks Pratt Over CFM for Engines Valued at $1.03 Billion |publisher= [[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]] |date= December 15, 2011 |access-date= 2017-03-11 |archive-date= 2016-06-17 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160617012616/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2011-12-14/jetblue-to-buy-pratt-whitney-engines |url-status= live }}</ref>
At the start of production in 2016, each GTF was costing PW $10m to build, more than the sale price, but was expected eventually to fall below $2 million per engine.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2016/06/13/pontifications-gtf-faces-steep-learning-curve-costs/ |title= Pontifications: GTF faces steep learning curve on costs |publisher= Leeham News |date= June 13, 2016 |archive-date= August 22, 2016 |access-date= June 13, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160822083119/https://leehamnews.com/2016/06/13/pontifications-gtf-faces-steep-learning-curve-costs/ |url-status= live }}</ref> MTU provides the first four stages of the high-pressure compressor, the low-pressure turbine and other components. In October 2016, MTU started to deliver the engine assembled on its line to Airbus.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/mtu-formally-opens-a320neo-engine-line-430607/ |title= MTU formally opens A320neo engine line |date= 21 October 2016 |work= Flight Global |archive-date= 22 October 2016 |access-date= 21 October 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20161022143706/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/mtu-formally-opens-a320neo-engine-line-430607/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

In November 2016, Pratt had fixed the engine-start problem and aimed to deliver 150 powerplants by year's end, 50 fewer than planned. This was because less than one-third of fan blades were passing inspection at the start of the year, a figure that rose to 75% as the year went on. Fuel-burn performance was 16% better than the IAE V2500 baseline, on target, and even 18% better in best cases. The 2017 delivery goal was set at 350 to 400 engines.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/pratt-sees-busy-year-end-it-targets-gtf-catch |title= Pratt Sees Busy Year-End As It Targets GTF Catch-Up |date= Nov 28, 2016 |author= Guy Norris |work= Aviation Week & Space Technology |archive-date= November 29, 2016 |access-date= November 28, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20161129023935/http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/pratt-sees-busy-year-end-it-targets-gtf-catch |url-status= live }}</ref>

The troubled introduction led customers to choose the [[CFM LEAP]], which won 396 A320neo orders compared to 39 for the GTF from January through early August 2017: 46% of the GTF-powered A320neos were out of service for at least one week in July 2017 compared with just 9% of those using the LEAP. The GTF's market share fell from 45% to 40% in 2016, but 1,523 planes ({{#expr:1523/(2179+1463+1523)*100round0}}%) were still undecided, and as of August 2017 Pratt had an 8,000-engine orderbook including 1,000 non-Airbus planes.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-08-22/pratt-s-10-billion-jet-engine-lags-ge-by-10-to-1-on-new-orders |title= Pratt's $10 Billion Jet Engine Lags GE by 10-to-1 on New Orders |author= Rick Clough |date= 22 Aug 2017 |work= Bloomberg |archive-date= 2017-08-23 |access-date= 2017-08-23 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170823162923/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-08-22/pratt-s-10-billion-jet-engine-lags-ge-by-10-to-1-on-new-orders |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Ultra high-bypass version ===

In 2010, Pratt & Whitney launched the development of an ultra high-bypass version, with a ratio higher than the PW1100G's 12.2:1 for the A320neo, to offer 20% better fuel consumption than a [[CFM56]]-7 and 25 dB less noise than the FAA's Stage 4.<!--<ref name=Flight13oct2017>-->

=== Starting times ===

The first delivery was to Lufthansa instead of [[Qatar Airways]] due to rotor bow, or thermal bowing, due to asymmetrical cooling after shut-down on the previous flight. Differences in temperature across the shaft section supporting the rotor lead to different thermal deformation of the shaft material, causing the rotor axis to bend; this results in an offset between the center of gravity of the bowed rotor and the bearing axis, causing a slight imbalance and potentially reducing the tight clearance between the rotor blade tips and the compressor wall. All production standard engines now feature a damper on the third and fourth shaft bearings to help stiffen the shaft and data from engines in service and under accelerated testing is expected to gradually reduce engine start times. According to P&W President Bob Leduc, "by the time we get to June (2016), it will be down to 200 seconds for start time and by the time we get to December (2016) we will be down to 150 seconds for start time".<ref>{{Cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/new-pw-president-has-nothing-hide-gtf-starter-issue |title= New P&W President Has 'Nothing To Hide' On GTF Starter Issue |date= 16 February 2016 |work= Aviation Week }}{{Dead link|date=May 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In an earnings briefing on 26 July the CEO of Pratt & Whitney's parent company [[United Technologies]] Gregory Hayes stated when asked about the start up issues on the PW1100G-JM; "On the technical stuff, I would tell you it is in the rearview mirror. The start time with the software drops have been pretty well addressed".<ref>{{cite news |url= https://finance.yahoo.com/news/edited-transcript-utx-earnings-conference-183800751.html |title= Edited Transcript of UTX earnings conference call or presentation 26-Jul-16 |work= Thomson Reuters Street Events |date= July 26, 2016 |publisher= Yahoo Finance |archive-date= November 29, 2016 |access-date= January 17, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20161129150859/http://finance.yahoo.com/news/edited-transcript-utx-earnings-conference-183800751.html |url-status= live }}</ref> Airbus group chief [[Tom Enders]] said while releasing Airbus's 2016 first half financial results that the first upgraded "golden engine" would be delivered to Lufthansa in early August 2016.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-delivery-of-pw-golden-a320neo-engine-immi-427892/ |title= Airbus: Delivery of P&W 'golden' A320neo engine imminent |date= 27 July 2016 |work= Flight Global |archive-date= 28 July 2016 |access-date= 28 July 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160728142413/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-delivery-of-pw-golden-a320neo-engine-immi-427892/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

Initially, the PW1000G start up sequence took about seven minutes, compared to one to two and a half minute startups on the similar [[CFM International CFM56|CFM56]] and [[IAE V2500]] engines; hardware fixes and software upgrades decreased the time required by a little over a minute, and cooling down both engines at the same time saved slightly over two minutes, for a total reduction of three and a half minutes. These modifications were included on new-build engines, as well as retrofitting existing units. Pratt & Whitney continued to improve start up times, with fuel-nozzle modifications and oil filling procedure changes expected to save another minute when introduced by the end of 2017.<ref name=AW170324/>

To create a better seal and reduce cooling time by 1 min, a cubic [[boron nitride]] coating was applied to the 11 integrally bladed rotors  tips: the [[A321neo]] production engines start times will be similar to the V2500.<ref name=Flight26May2017>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/flight-test-a321neo-stretches-its-legs-437215/ |title= Flight test: A321neo stretches its legs |date= 26 May 2017 |author= Mike Gerzanics |work= Flight Global |archive-date= 29 December 2018 |access-date= 26 May 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181229223759/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/flight-test-a321neo-stretches-its-legs-437215/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Engine removals ===
[[File:IGO A320neo F-WWII!6849 22dec15 LFBO.jpg|thumb|[[IndiGo]] A320neo waiting for its engines]]

As [[IndiGo]] and [[Go Air]] operate in a [[humid]], hot, [[Air pollution|polluted]] and [[Sea spray|salty]] environment, 42 engines were prematurely removed from those companies' aircraft by 24 February, with more removals scheduled, after warnings, mandatory checks, and possible repairs were due after only three flight hours instead of ten. 28 engine removals were due to an air [[Seal (mechanical)|seal]] leakage in the third [[Bearing (mechanical)|bearing]], which allowed metal particles to enter the oil system, triggering detectors. Pratt & Whitney discovered these issues in 2015 and revised the design in 2016 after the 160th engine with improved bearing compartments and [[Damping ratio|damping]] for the third and fourth bearings to offset the rotor-bow, with the repairs retrofitted on-wing after testing at Airbus and Pratt.<ref name=AW170324/> Boosting durability of the third bearing compartment air seal, the upgraded carbon seal package was certified on April 12 and can be retrofitted over a typical night stop.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://atwonline.com/engines/pratt-whitney-begins-a320neo-engine-seal-upgrade |title= Pratt & Whitney begins A320neo engine seal upgrade |date= Apr 20, 2017 |author= Guy Norris |work= Air Transport World |publisher= Aviation Week |archive-date= April 21, 2017 |access-date= April 20, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170421025752/http://atwonline.com/engines/pratt-whitney-begins-a320neo-engine-seal-upgrade |url-status= live }}</ref>

Thirteen engine removals were due to [[borescope]] inspections revealing blocked cooling holes in [[combustion chamber]] panels, apparently due to saltier air, and Pratt & Whitney developed and tested a more durable [[combustor]] design to address a tone problem, to be introduced in September.<ref name=AW170324>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/airlines-praise-airbus-a320neo-performance-engine-issues-remain |title= Airlines Praise Airbus A320neo Performance, But Engine Issues Remain |date= Mar 24, 2017 |author= Jens Flottau |author2= Guy Norris |work= Aviation Week & Space Technology |archive-date= September 11, 2018 |access-date= March 28, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180911234857/http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/airlines-praise-airbus-a320neo-performance-engine-issues-remain |url-status= live }}</ref>
[[Spirit Airlines]] reported that the [[bleed air]] system froze shut on occasion due to cold temperatures on four of its five A320neos, a problem also experienced by IndiGo, leading Spirit to impose a {{convert|30000|ft|m}} ceiling on their aircraft.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://airwaysmag.com/airlines/report-spirit-a320neo-engine-troubles/ |title= Report: Spirit A320neo Fleet Suffering PW1000G Engine Challenges |work= Airways Magazine |date= 10 April 2017 |author= Benjamin Bearup |archive-date= 6 September 2018 |access-date= 11 April 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180906084939/https://airwaysmag.com/airlines/report-spirit-a320neo-engine-troubles/ |url-status= live }}</ref>  To avoid troubles with the P&W1100G engines, [[JetBlue Airways]] switched its first three Airbus A321neos in 2018 to [[A321ceo]]s, deferring delivery of its first A321neos to 2019 among its order for 60.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/jetblue-switches-a321neos-as-pratt-troubles-persist-436532/ |title= JetBlue switches A321neos as Pratt troubles persist |date= 25 Apr 2017 |work= Flight Global |archive-date= 26 April 2017 |access-date= 25 April 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170426062036/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/jetblue-switches-a321neos-as-pratt-troubles-persist-436532/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

In 2017, IndiGo had to ground seven planes, two in May, four in June and one in July after, their engines out of service, waiting for upgrades: a lack of spare parts—grounding also [[All Nippon Airways]] and [[Hong Kong Express Airways]] A320s—has been compounded by a new Indian tax on goods and services, impeding imports.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-07-13/indigo-grounds-at-least-seven-jets-to-await-pratt-engine-fixes |title= Pratt Engine Fixes Prompt IndiGo to Ground Seven Airbus Planes |author= Anurag Kotoky |author2= Rick Clough |author3= Benjamin D Katz |date= 13 Jul 2017 |work= Bloomberg |archive-date= 2017-08-23 |access-date= 2017-08-23 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170823161253/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-07-13/indigo-grounds-at-least-seven-jets-to-await-pratt-engine-fixes |url-status= live }}</ref>
With removals without sufficient spare engines available, IndiGo had to ground as many as nine jets on some days. The disruptions to operations were compensated for by Pratt & Whitney which at the time said it would be able to sort out the issues within one and a half years.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-07-31/pratt-pays-top-a320neo-customer-compensation-as-glitches-persist |title= Pratt's Woes With Engines Spur Compensation to Biggest User |author= Anurag Kotoky |date= 31 Jul 2017 |work= Bloomberg |archive-date= 2017-08-23 |access-date= 2017-08-23 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170823164020/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-07-31/pratt-pays-top-a320neo-customer-compensation-as-glitches-persist |url-status= live }}</ref> Indigo had to replace 69 engines from mid 2016 till early 2018.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-02-11/indigo-says-has-made-69-pratt-engine-replacements-in-18-months-jdiqawr6 |title= IndiGo Says Has Made 69 Pratt Engine Replacements in 18 Months |author= Anurag Kotoky |date= 11 Feb 2018 |agency= Bloomberg |archive-date= 2018-02-12 |access-date= 2018-02-12 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180212203723/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-02-11/indigo-says-has-made-69-pratt-engine-replacements-in-18-months-jdiqawr6 |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Knife edge seal ===

In February 2018, after in-flight failures of PW1100G with its high pressure [[Gas turbine engine compressors|compressor]] aft hub modified – apparently problems of its knife edge [[mechanical seal|seal]], the [[EASA]] and Airbus grounded some [[A320neo family]] aircraft until they are fitted with spares.<ref name=Flight9feb2018>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/in-flight-failures-prompt-emergency-call-for-pw-pow-445789/ |title= In-flight failures prompt emergency call for P&W-powered A320neos |date= 9 Feb 2018 |author= Stephen Trimble |work= Flightglobal |archive-date= 11 February 2018 |access-date= 11 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180211131414/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/in-flight-failures-prompt-emergency-call-for-pw-pow-445789/ |url-status= live }}</ref> Later, Airbus decided to stop accepting additional PW1100G engines for A320neo aircraft.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://atwonline.com/engines/airbus-stops-accepting-pw1100g-engines-a320neo-aircraft|title=Airbus stops accepting PW1100G engines for A320neo aircraft|access-date=2018-02-11|date=February 10, 2018|author=Jens Flottau and Aaron Karp|work=Air Transport World|archive-date=2018-02-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211075323/http://atwonline.com/engines/airbus-stops-accepting-pw1100g-engines-a320neo-aircraft|url-status=live}}</ref>
Despite the part failure that could hold up engine deliveries to Airbus until April, P&W reaffirmed its 2018 delivery goal of doubling its 2017 rate of 374 engines as nearly 100 engines delivered to Airbus are problematic, including 43 in service.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-reaffirms-2018-gtf-delivery-goal-despite-part-fa-445968/ |title= P&W reaffirms 2018 GTF delivery goal despite part failure |date= 16 Feb 2018 |author= Stephen Trimble |work= Flightglobal |archive-date= 16 February 2018 |access-date= 16 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180216044540/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/pw-reaffirms-2018-gtf-delivery-goal-despite-part-fa-445968/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

To solve the issue, a revised configuration with a mature and approved design will be released from early March engine deliveries.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://newsroom.pw.utc.com/2018-02-21-Pratt-Whitney-Implements-Solution-to-PW1100G-JM |title= Pratt & Whitney Implements Solution to PW1100G-JM |date= Feb 21, 2018 |publisher= Pratt & Whitney |access-date= 2018-02-22 |archive-date= 2018-02-22 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180222004629/http://newsroom.pw.utc.com/2018-02-21-Pratt-Whitney-Implements-Solution-to-PW1100G-JM |url-status= live }}</ref>
The EASA and FAA imposed flying A320neos with mixed engines and forbid [[ETOPS]], but the [[Indian DGCA]] went further and grounded all A320neo with an affected engine.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2018/03/14/pratt-whitneys-indian-trouble/ |title= Pratt & Whitney's Indian trouble |author= Bjorn Fehrm |date= March 14, 2018 |work= Leeham}}</ref>
The design flaw will cost Pratt & Whitney $50 million to resolve.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/fixing-faulty-gtf-seal-to-cost-50-million-pw-446840/ |title= Fixing faulty GTF seal to cost $50 million: P&W |date= 16 March 2018 |author= Stephen Trimble |work= Flightglobal |archive-date= 17 March 2018 |access-date= 17 March 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180317165154/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/fixing-faulty-gtf-seal-to-cost-50-million-pw-446840/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
P&W will replace the seals in the 55 engines delivered to Airbus and in the 43 in-service GTFs, as the target of 750 deliveries in 2018 seems more remote.<ref name=AIN16mar2018>{{cite news |url= https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-03-16/pratt-whitney-details-gtf-recovery-schedule |title= Pratt & Whitney Details GTF Recovery Schedule |author= Chris Kjelgaard |date= March 16, 2018 |work= AIN |archive-date= 2018-03-20 |access-date= 2018-03-19 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180320043907/https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-03-16/pratt-whitney-details-gtf-recovery-schedule |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Engine vibrations===

By September 2018, the A320neo's PW1100Gs were experiencing increasing engine [[vibration]]s, sometimes before 1,000 flight hours and mostly at high power settings in the [[climb phase]], requiring an early engine change.<!--<ref name=AvWeek6sep2018>-->
[[Lufthansa]]'s A320neos were [[Aircraft on ground|grounded]] 254 days since first delivery, 13 times worse than for its [[Airbus A320 family|A320ceos]], 78% of the time due to engine issues as 14 unplanned engine changes were made. In September 2018 its A320neos [[Rental utilization|utilization]] was half of its A320ceos.<!--<ref name=AvWeek6sep2018>-->
By the end of November, Airbus planned to explain the [[root cause analysis|root cause]] and give an in-depth [[analysis]] by the end of 2018.<ref name=AvWeek6sep2018>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/a320neo-engine-vibration-issue-hits-lufthansa-ops |title= A320neo Engine Vibration Issue Hits Lufthansa Ops |date= Sep 6, 2018 |author= Jens Flottau |work= Aviation Week Network |archive-date= September 10, 2018 |access-date= September 9, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180910141027/http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/a320neo-engine-vibration-issue-hits-lufthansa-ops |url-status= live }}</ref>  Pratt & Whitney stated the A220's and Embraer E2's PW1500G/PW1900Gs are free from the issue and that less than 2% of PW1100Gs are affected while {{#expr:140+42}} GTF-powered A320/A321neos have been delivered.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a320neo-operators-affected-by-pw1100g-vibration-issu-451814/ |title= A320neo operators affected by PW1100G vibration issue |date= 11 Sep 2018 |author= Michael Gubisch |work= Flightglobal}}</ref>

[[File:JetBlue Airbus A220 N3194J take off Boston July 2025.webm|thumb|right|The PW1500G's whale-like noise can be heard at the beginning of this video of a [[JetBlue Airways|JetBlue]] Airbus A220 taking off from [[Logan International Airport|Boston]].]]

In 2018 some PW1500G engines were reported as emitting "a strange howling noise" similar to that of a whale by people below the aircraft as it made its landing approach. Pratt & Whitney had not established what was causing the noise at that time. <ref>{{cite web | work = Traveller | place = [[Australia|AU]] | url = https://www.traveller.com.au/airbus-a220-whisperjet-is-too-loud-according-to-zurich-residents-h17jqc | title = Anger as new Airbus A220 'Whisperjet' judged too loud | date = 6 November 2018 | access-date = 17 November 2022 | archive-date = 17 November 2022 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20221117095852/https://www.traveller.com.au/airbus-a220-whisperjet-is-too-loud-according-to-zurich-residents-h17jqc | url-status = live }}</ref> In a podcast in April 2020, Graham Webb, the Vice President and General Manager of the regional jet geared turbofan engine program at Pratt and Whitney claimed that the engine noise was caused by a "low power transient combustor tone" which generally occurs on approach when the engine is at low or idle power. Under those conditions, the flame front inside the combustor behaves in a way that causes pressure perturbations that interact with the walls of the combustor to create the whale sound. The noise has no repercussions on the operation of the engine. <ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Petchenik |first=Ian |date=2020-12-04 |title=AvTalk Episode 99: Solving the mystery of the whale song |url=https://www.flightradar24.com/blog/avtalk-podcast/avtalk-episode-99-solving-the-mystery-of-the-whale-song/ |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=Flightradar24 Blog |language=en-US}}</ref>

By October 2018 about 10 P&W-powered A320neos were typically grounded for repairs at any given time.<ref>{{cite web|work= Niki aviation|url= https://www.nikiaviation.com/files/brochures/New_Zealand_Aviation_News_2018.pdf|title= Engine vibrations unsatisfactory|year= 2018|publisher= [[New Zealand aviation news]]|access-date= 2019-06-09|archive-date= 2019-10-21|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191021054931/https://www.nikiaviation.com/files/brochures/New_Zealand_Aviation_News_2018.pdf|url-status= dead}}</ref>

===Excessive corrosion===
Pratt & Whitney has reduced life limits on PW1500G (installed on the Airbus A220) and PW1900G (installed on Embraer E190/E195-E2) high-pressure compressor front hubs after corrosion was discovered during routine engine overhaul. This corrosion reduces the low-cycle fatigue capability and may lead to cracking before the component reaches its life limit.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/corrosion-cuts-life-limit-of-a220-and-e2-compressor-458694/ |title= Airbus A220 and Embraer E2 operators are being advised of cycle limit amendments to the high-pressure compressor hub on their Pratt & Whitney engines |date= 4 June 2019 |work= Flightglobal |archive-date= 8 June 2019 |access-date= 9 June 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190608052508/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/corrosion-cuts-life-limit-of-a220-and-e2-compressor-458694/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

On 25 July 2019, an Airbus A220-300 operated by Swiss International Air Lines had an [[Turbine engine failure|engine failure]] and diverted to [[Paris–Charles de Gaulle]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://avherald.com/h?article=4cac778d&opt=0|title=Incident: Swiss BCS3 near Paris on Jul 25th 2019, engine shut down in flight|website=Av herald|date=Jul 25, 2019|access-date=November 7, 2019|archive-date=March 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210324015055/http://avherald.com/h?article=4cac778d&opt=0|url-status=live}}</ref> The low-pressure compressor of one its PW1500G engines disintegrated while climbing through 32,000 ft.<ref>{{cite news|title=Public help sought to find fallen Swiss A220 engine parts|url =https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/public-help-sought-to-find-fallen-swiss-a220-engine-460377/|date=August 20, 2019|author=David Kaminiski-Morrow|work=FlightGlobal}}</ref>

On 16 September 2019, a similar accident happened just before reaching 35,000 ft and the crew returned to [[Geneva Airport|Geneva]]. The inspection has shown that "stage-one rotor in the low-pressure compressor had separated and there was a hole in the compressor case".<ref>{{cite news|title=Second Swiss A220 suffers similar engine rotor failure|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/second-swiss-a220-suffers-similar-engine-rotor-failu-460991/|date=September 20, 2019|author=David Kaminiski-Morrow|work=Flight Global|archive-date=November 4, 2019|access-date=October 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191104124643/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/second-swiss-a220-suffers-similar-engine-rotor-failu-460991/|url-status=live}}</ref> On 26 September the [[Federal Aviation Administration|FAA]] issued an [[Airworthiness Directive]] mandating [[borescope]] inspections on the engines.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rgl.faa.gov/Regulatory_and_Guidance_Library/rgad.nsf/0/c7583adc61e5955a86258481004b6dd6/$FILE/2019-19-11.pdf|title=Airworthiness Directive 2019-11-11|publisher=FAA|date=September 26, 2019|access-date=2019-11-07|archive-date=2019-10-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191015211303/http://rgl.faa.gov/Regulatory_and_Guidance_Library/rgad.nsf/0/c7583adc61e5955a86258481004b6dd6/$FILE/2019-19-11.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 15 October 2019, another engine failed and the crew diverted to Paris-Charles de Gaulle, after which Swiss withdrew its fleet for inspection.<ref>{{cite news|title=Third Swiss A220 failure spurs urgent engine checks|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/third-swiss-a220-failure-spurs-urgent-engine-checks-461504/|date=October 15, 2019|author=David Kaminiski-Morrow|work=FlightGlobal|archive-date=October 22, 2019|access-date=October 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022104119/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/third-swiss-a220-failure-spurs-urgent-engine-checks-461504/|url-status=live}}</ref> Swiss returned some aircraft to flight status the same day after engine checks and planned to restore flight operations by 17 October.<ref>{{cite news |work= Flight global |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/swiss-gradually-starts-returning-a220s-to-flight-sta-461509/ |title= Swiss gradually starts returning A220s to flight status |date= 15 Oct 2019 |author= David Kaminski-Morrow |archive-date= 22 October 2019 |access-date= 7 November 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191022100857/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/swiss-gradually-starts-returning-a220s-to-flight-sta-461509/ |url-status= live }}</ref> A [[software update]] may have caused damaging [[vibrations]] of fast-moving parts, leading to the failures.<ref>{{cite news|title=Exclusive: Software link suspected in Airbus A220 engine blowouts—sources|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-airbus-a220-exclusive/exclusive-software-link-suspected-in-airbus-a220-engine-blowouts-sources-idUSKBN1X31ST|date=October 24, 2019|author=Tim Hepher|work=Reuters|archive-date=October 24, 2019|access-date=October 24, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191024180643/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-airbus-a220-exclusive/exclusive-software-link-suspected-in-airbus-a220-engine-blowouts-sources-idUSKBN1X31ST|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[autothrottle]] for the climb over this altitude before engaging it again in cruise.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a220-operators-told-to-limit-engine-thrust-at-high-a-461843/ |title= A220 operators told to limit engine thrust at high altitude |date= 28 Oct 2019 |author= Low Pressure Spool, with a nominal speed of 10,600 [[RPM]], with the fan geared with a ratio of 1:3.0625 (nominal speed {{#expr:10600/3.0625round0}} RPM).<ref name= "PW1500tcds">{{cite web |title=Type The engines involved in the July and September incidents had 154 and 230 cycles, respectively, while the October failure occurred to an engine with 1,654 cycles since new but within 300 cycles after an [[FADEC|electronic engine-control]] update. Pratt & Whitney recommends inspections on engines with up to 300 cycles after the update.<ref>{{cite news|title=A220 engine checks revised after high-cycle Swiss failure|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a220-engine-checks-revised-after-high-cycle-swiss-fa-461871/|date=October 30, 2019|author=David Kaminiski-Morrow|work=Flight Global|archive-date=October 30, 2019|access-date=November 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030153101/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a220-engine-checks-revised-after-high-cycle-swiss-fa-461871/|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 12 February 2020, another PW1500G suffered an uncontained engine failure on an A220-300 belonging to Latvia's [[airBaltic]] during flight BT-677 from Riga, Latvia to Malaga, Spain.<ref>{{cite web|title=Incident: Baltic BCS3 near Bordeaux on Feb 12th 2020, uncontained engine failure|url=https://avherald.com/h?article=4d338076&opt=0|date=February 12, 2020|work=Aviation Herald|access-date=February 18, 2020|archive-date=May 4, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504232115/http://avherald.com/h?article=4d338076&opt=0|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url= https://skiesmag.com/news/another-engine-failure-on-the-airbus-a220/|title= Another engine failure on the Airbus A220|date= Feb 13, 2020|work= Skies Magazine|access-date= April 12, 2021|archive-date= April 10, 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210410203420/https://skiesmag.com/news/another-engine-failure-on-the-airbus-a220/|url-status= live}}</ref>

Following these Airbus A220 PW1500G failures, the similar PW1900G electronic control software was upgraded for the [[Embraer E195-E2]] in 2021.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/safety/e195-e2-engine-software-upgrade-ordered-after-a220-failure-incidents/143011.article|title=E195-E2 engine software upgrade ordered after A220 failure incidents|first=David|last=Kaminski-Morrow|website=Flight Global|date=24 March 2021|archive-date=10 April 2021|access-date=12 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210410203421/https://www.flightglobal.com/safety/e195-e2-engine-software-upgrade-ordered-after-a220-failure-incidents/143011.article|url-status=live}}</ref>

To address the issue for the PW1500G, Pratt & Whitney developed a software update for the engine control system that was specifically designed to improve engine performance during all flight operations. The update was first approved by the [[Federal Aviation Authority|FAA]] in March 2019, and was subsequently incorporated into the engines of a number of Airbus A220 aircraft.<ref name="prnewswire_300780225">{{cite press release |url= https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/pratt--whitney-initiates-comprehensive-review-of-pw1500g-engine-after-in-flight-shutdowns-300780225.html |title= Pratt & Whitney Initiates Comprehensive Review of PW1500G Engine After in-Flight Shutdowns  |agency= [[PR Newswire]] |date= 2019-01-18 |access-date=2023-06-12 }}</ref> The software update addressed the root cause of the compression stall problem by adjusting the engine's control logic to provide more consistent and stable airflow through the engine core. This was achieved by optimizing the engine's inlet guide vanes and airflow sensors, as well as altering the engine's response to certain flight conditions.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://aviationweek.com/air-transport/safety-ops-regulation/pratt-whitney-deploys-fix-a220-engine-flaw |title=Pratt & Whitney Deploys Fix for A220 Engine Flaw |work=Aviation Week |publisher=Aviation Week Network |date=2019-05-09 |access-date=2023-06-12 }}{{Dead link|date=May 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Pratt & Whitney also conducted a comprehensive review of the PW1500G engine and its components to identify any other potential issues. Extensive testing and data analysis have resulted in further modifications to the engine's design and performance characteristics.<ref name = "prnewswire_300780225"/>

As of June 2023, there have been no other reported incidents of compression stalls on PW1500G-powered aircraft since the software update was implemented. 

On 23 December 2024, an Airbus A220-300, operating as [[Swiss International Air Lines Flight 1885]] experienced an engine failure at FL400, leading to smoke entering the cabin and forcing the aircraft to divert to [[Graz Airport]]. Of the 79 occupants, 1 died and 21 were injured.

extract:
The Pratt & Whitney PW1000G family, also marketed as the Pratt & Whitney GTF (geared turbofan), is a family of high-bypass geared turbofan engines produced by Pratt & Whitney. The various models can generate 15,000 to 33,000 pounds-force (67 to 147 kilonewtons) of thrust. As of 2025, they are used on the Airbus A220, Airbus A320neo family, and Embraer E-Jet E2. They were also used on new Yakovlev MC-21s until exports to Russia were stopped as part of the international sanctions during the invasion of Ukraine.
Following years of development and testing on various demonstrators, the program officially launched in 2008 with the PW1200G destined for the later-canceled Mitsubishi SpaceJet. The first successful flight test occurred later that year. The PW1500G variant, designed for the A220, became the first certified engine in 2013. P&W is estimated to have spent $10 billion to develop the engine family. The type certificate for the PW1100G is held by International Aero Engines while the other versions are held by Pratt & Whitney.
Unlike traditional turbofan engines whose single shaft forces all components to turn at the same speed, the PW1000G has a gearbox between the fan and the low-pressure core. This allows each section to operate at its optimal speed. Pratt & Whitney says this enables the PW1000G to use 16% less fuel and produce 75% less noise than previous generation engines.
The engine family initially garnered interest from airlines due to its fuel efficiency, but technical problems have hurt its standing in the market. For example, early problems with the PW1100G variant, which powers the A320neo family, grounded aircraft and caused in-flight failures. Some engines were built with contaminated powdered metal, requiring repairs of 250 to 300 days. Some airlines chose the CFM LEAP engine instead.
